name: Indapamide

lead: Indapamide is a blood-pressure water pill that is occasionally raised in depuffing talk as a way to reduce fluid retention and get a less puffy face.

It acts mainly on the distal tubule of the kidney to increase sodium and water excretion, with an elimination half-life of about 14-18 hours. Large trials, including PROGRESS, ADVANCE and HYVET, tested indapamide-based regimens in stroke survivors, people with type 2 diabetes and adults aged 80 and over; none addressed appearance or depuffing.

paras: It is a prescription tablet, taken once daily in its medical use for high blood pressure and heart-failure fluid retention. Water loss begins the same day it is taken.

Common effects include low potassium, fatigue and dizziness on standing. It is avoided in sulfonamide hypersensitivity and severe kidney or liver failure, and caution is advised with lithium and QT-prolonging drugs. It is prescription-only.

angle.text: Indapamide is occasionally raised as a water-pill option for a less puffy face. It makes the kidneys excrete more sodium and water, so less fluid is held in the tissues. Large trials have studied it for stroke prevention and blood pressure, not appearance.

lead: Indapamide is a thiazide-like diuretic used mainly for hypertension and for edema from congestive heart failure. It was patented in 1968, approved for medical use in 1977, and appears on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[1]

Large outcome trials, including PROGRESS, ADVANCE and HYVET, tested indapamide-based regimens, often together with perindopril, in stroke survivors, people with type 2 diabetes and adults aged 80 and over.[2][3][4] It has not been studied for cosmetic use.

paras: Indapamide lowers blood pressure and is used for edema in congestive heart failure.[1][5] In trials, a perindopril-indapamide regimen reduced stroke in high-risk patients (PROGRESS), and the HYVET trial in people aged 80 or older reported lower all-cause mortality with treatment, though not a significant reduction in cardiac deaths.[1][2][4]

Common effects are low potassium, fatigue, orthostatic hypotension and allergic reactions; potassium and uric acid should be monitored. Contraindications include sulfonamide hypersensitivity, severe kidney or liver failure and low potassium, and caution is advised with lithium and QT-prolonging drugs.[1][5]
Indapamide is taken orally, is roughly 71-79% protein-bound and metabolised in the liver; the half-life is about 14-18 hours.[1]

Indapamide is prescription-only in the UK and EU and is listed among WADA-prohibited substances on Wikipedia.[1] The sources reviewed contain no substantive discussion of it in looksmaxxing communities.

No studies found on indapamide for facial depuffing or other appearance goals. Large trials in hypertension, stroke and diabetes include PROGRESS, ADVANCE and HYVET, and a registered trial compares it with hydrochlorothiazide in older adults with renal insufficiency.[2][3][4][6]
